name: CRGO Electrical Steel & Transformer Core Localisation
scope: India's import-dependent CRGO / amorphous transformer-steel supply chain, the DGTR anti-dumping probe, JSW JFE capacity build-out, and the listed steel makers, core processors and transformer makers exposed to it.

summary.one_line: India still imports about 90% of its 400-450 kt/yr CRGO need. The DGTR case is past mid-way with no preliminary findings, and statutory final findings are due by about Jun 2027. JSW Steel's JV capacity arrives only from FY28. The listed processors kept de-rating this week: Jay Bee is -53% YoY and Vilas is now negative over both 6 and 12 months.
key_points: Demand is about 400-450 kt a year against 40-50 kt of domestic output, so nearly 90% is imported (S1, S3). Imports of the products under investigation were worth $821.5m in FY26, up 15.5% YoY. China supplied 33.6% of the wider CRGO category, Japan 31.4%, Russia 20.6% and Korea 6.5% (S4).

DGTR opened the anti-dumping case on 22 Jun 2026 (F. No. 6/17/2026-DGTR). It covers CRGO and amorphous metal from China, Japan, Korea and Russia, on a petition by JSW JFE Electrical Steel Nashik (S5). The period of investigation is Apr 2025-Mar 2026, and the applicant wants duties applied up to 90 days retrospectively (S6). Under Rule 17, final findings are due within one year of initiation, extendable by six months, which points to about Jun 2027 or Dec 2027 at the latest (S26). As of this edition we found no preliminary findings.

By 3 Sep 2026, 98 interested-party entries had registered. User-industry or importer registrants include listed CG Power, Hitachi Energy India, Indo Tech Transformers, TARIL, Atlanta Electricals and BHEL. Mangal Electrical is the only listed name filed as a 'supporter to domestic industry' (S5).

JSW JFE plans to expand Nashik from 50 to 250 ktpa and Vijayanagar to 100 ktpa. Total spend is Rs 5,845 cr, with phases commissioning from FY2028 to a total of 350 ktpa (S7, S8). Completion of the Nashik tunnel furnaces is targeted for Q1 2027 (S9).

The JV is still immaterial for JSW Steel. JSW reported Q2 FY27 consolidated revenue of Rs 54,486 cr, up 31% YoY, and PAT of Rs 5,359 cr (published 23 Oct 2026). Coverage of the results and PL Capital's 24 Oct note made no mention of electrical steel (S21, S28).

Lower CRGO prices are still hurting processor realisations. Mangal's Q1 FY27 CRGO volume rose about 32% while realisations fell about 18% YoY (S25). Vilas's Q1 FY27 revenue grew 18.2% even though CRGO prices fell about 20% (S13). Jay Bee's FY26 EBITDA margin fell to 6.2% from 11.7% (S14).

The market has not re-rated the theme; it has de-rated it further. On 28 Oct 2026 Jay Bee was -53.3% over 1 year (S19). Around 30 Oct 2026 Vilas was about -22% to -26% over both 6 months and 1 year (S18). JSW Steel was -0.2% over 6 months and +4.8% over 1 year on 16 Oct 2026 (S20). We still found no broker note that frames any of these as a CRGO play.

for_investors.title: Who benefits
points: JSW Steel, through its 50:50 JSW JFE JV, is the petitioner and the only domestic CRGO producer with standing in the case (S3, S5). A duty would support pricing as Nashik and Vijayanagar ramp toward 350 ktpa from FY28 (S8).

Processors with domestic sourcing options. ICRA notes Vilas has diversified to domestic CRGO suppliers since FY2021 (S12). Mangal Electrical, a 16,200 MT CRGO processor, registered as a supporter of the domestic industry (S5, S22).

Proterial's Metglas amorphous plant at Sri City (about 30 kt/yr, a 74:26 JV with unlisted Shirdi Sai Electricals) would be local supply inside any duty wall (S16). Its targeted Oct 2026 start had not been confirmed as of this edition.

for_investors.title: Who is hurt / risks
points: Transformer makers that import CRGO: Indo Tech is registered as both user and importer, and TARIL as importer (S5). CRGO is about 33-35% of their raw-material cost, according to TARIL (S10).

Small processors carry the price pass-through risk on thin margins. Jay Bee's FY26 EBITDA margin was 6.2% (S14). ICRA flags Vilas's exposure to CRGO price and availability, its 80-90 day inventory and its ~45-55% customer concentration (S12).
For JSW Steel the payoff is small and late. The JV is unlisted and 50% owned (S7), JSW booked Rs 54,486 cr of revenue in Q2 FY27 alone (S21), and new capacity only starts from FY2028 (S8).

for_investors.title: What to watch
points: Any DGTR preliminary findings, then final findings, which are due by about Jun 2027 (extendable to about Dec 2027) (S26). After that comes the Ministry of Finance decision (S24).

Sep-quarter / H1 FY27 results from Vilas, Jay Bee and Mangal, expected in Nov 2026. Watch whether Vilas holds its 45-50% FY27 growth guidance (S13) and whether Jay Bee meets its 16,000-18,000 t volume guidance (S14).
Confirmation of the Metglas Sri City start (S16) and the Nashik furnace's Q1 2027 completion target (S9).

kpis.label: DGTR final-findings deadline
kpis.sub: 1 yr from 22 Jun 2026 initiation, +6 mo extendable (S5, S26)

subsections.title: What CRGO and amorphous metal are

blocks.text: Cold-rolled grain-oriented (CRGO) electrical steel and amorphous metal are the core materials of power and distribution transformers. About 98% of CRGO output goes into transformers (S11). Amorphous ribbon, such as Proterial's Metglas, cuts transformer no-load losses and can reduce standby power use by roughly one-third compared with conventional electrical sheet (S16). In the case initiation, DGTR took a prima facie view that the two are substitutable, which is why amorphous metal is in scope even though the applicant makes only CRGO. Interested parties may contest that view (S6).

The supply chain has three layers: steel mills that make CRGO coil; processors that slit, cut and assemble it into laminations and cores (Vilas, Jay Bee, Mangal, and TARIL's POSCO Poggenamp unit); and transformer makers (S10, S12, S22). Sources disagree on CRGO's cost share because they measure it on different bases. TARIL puts it at about 33-35% of transformer raw-material cost (S10). TERI puts it at 15-20% of a standard transformer's bill of materials, while an MSME source quoted 40-50% (S11).

blocks.text: BIS licensing already works as a non-tariff gate. Imports must comply with IS 3024, and in 2024 the expiry or non-renewal of BIS licences for major Chinese exporters halted some shipments. That produced an acute shortage, especially of Hi-B grade, and user industry appealed for imports to be allowed until domestic output began (S27). GTRI says that because imports already need BIS certification, the anti-dumping dispute is about price, not quality (S1, S3).

blocks.text: GTRI raises a methodology objection. DGTR treated China as a non-market economy and, citing a lack of domestic price data for Japan, Korea and Russia, largely used the Indian producer's cost as the benchmark for all four countries (S3). GTRI also notes that CRGO was previously left out of safeguard duties because of continued import dependence (S1). The Indian Steel Association counters that CRGO needs 7-10 times the investment per tonne of conventional greenfield steel, and that unchecked subsidised imports could undermine foreign investor confidence (S11).

Opposition is broad. DGTR's 3 Sep 2026 list contains 98 interested-party entries, including the Embassy of Japan, the Russian Ministry of Economic Development, IEEMA, KOSA and the China Iron and Steel Association. Several listed transformer makers registered as user industry or importers (S5). Indian rules set no fixed deadline for preliminary findings or provisional duty (S26), so the timing of any interim duty is uncertain.

blocks.title: Domestic electrical-steel capacity: today vs announced
blocks.source: Source: GTRI (S1), Wire & Cable India / The Machine Maker (S7, S8), machinist.in (S16); cumulative sum is our arithmetic

blocks.text: Our arithmetic: even with the full 350 ktpa from the JV and 30 kt of amorphous ribbon, announced capacity of about 380 kt would sit below today's 400-450 kt demand estimate (S1, S8, S16). The grid plan more than doubles transformer capacity, from 1,290 GVA in 2024 to 2,342 GVA by 2032 (S11). Imports therefore look set to remain the marginal source of supply through at least FY28-30.

blocks.text: Falling CRGO prices have so far hurt processor realisations more than any duty could. All three report volume growth well ahead of price-driven revenue (S13, S14, S25). A duty would reverse the price trend. Processors that can pass costs through would see inventory gains; any lag in pass-through would compress margins that ICRA already flags as sensitive to CRGO prices and forex, with no formal hedging (S12). Neither Vilas nor Jay Bee appears on DGTR's interested-party list, while Mangal backs the petition (S5).

JSW Steel holds 50% of the JV; JFE holds the other half (S7). JSW Steel's Q2 FY27 consolidated revenue was Rs 54,486 cr, with PAT of Rs 5,359 cr, published 23 Oct 2026 (S21). Results coverage and PL Capital's 24 Oct note discuss the JFE JV only in the context of the BPSL steel unit and do not mention electrical steel (S21, S28). As an illustration only (our arithmetic, not a forecast): 350 ktpa at the Rs 190-195/kg CRGO price Vilas cites (S13) gives roughly Rs 6,700 cr of gross revenue for the whole JV. That is about 3% of JSW Steel's annualised Q2 revenue before applying JSW's 50% share, and would not arrive before FY28-30.

Downstream, DGTR registrants include CG Power (as user industry and as exporter/producer), Hitachi Energy India, Indo Tech (user and importer), TARIL (importer), Atlanta Electricals and BHEL (S5). TARIL has partly hedged through backward integration: in Jan 2025 it bought 51% of POSCO Poggenamp Electrical Steel, a 24,000 t/yr CRGO processor (S10). TERI estimates that a 10% rise in CRGO prices adds 1.5-3% to transformer cost (S11).

items: GTRI (Ajay Srivastava): a duty raises transformer and grid costs while giving only limited protection, because domestic output is under one-tenth of demand. He calls the four-country common Indian cost benchmark questionable (S1, S3).
TERI (Alekhya Datta): a 10% rise in CRGO prices adds 1.5-3% to transformer cost and a 20% rise adds 3-6% (S11).
Indian Steel Association (Alok Sahay): domestic CRGO capacity is capital-intensive, and subsidised imports threaten investment (S11).
An MSME federation official, speaking anonymously, says JSW is 'the only beneficiary' of the probe (S11).
ICRA (Vilas, Jul 2025): reaffirmed [ICRA]A- (Stable)/A2+. It cites interest cover of 29.7x against working-capital intensity, customer concentration and exposure to CRGO prices (S12).
PL Capital (JSW Steel Q2 FY27, 24 Oct 2026): its thesis rests on volumes, the capex pipeline and the BPSL/JFE expansion, with no electrical-steel element (S28).

blocks.text: Coverage remains thin. We again found no sell-side initiation or sector note framing JSW Steel, Vilas, Jay Bee or Mangal as a CRGO localisation play. Discussion is limited to think tanks, trade press, a rating rationale and retail analysis sites (S14). The theme is still undiscovered.

subsections.title: Has the market priced it in?

blocks.caption: Stock performance (latest dated readings found; today's numbers are on the dashboard)

blocks.text: Change since last week: Vilas's 6-month return has turned from +15.6% (23 Sep reading) to roughly -22% to -26%. Its price was Rs 337.65, near the low end of its 52-week range (S18). Jay Bee traded at Rs 81.20 on 28 Oct, down 31.4% year-to-date (S19). Neither processor has re-rated on the probe.

items: The duty could be rejected or diluted. Opposition is organised, including foreign governments, industry associations and large user-industry registrants (S5), and GTRI and TERI point to the cost to the grid (S1, S11).
Timing mismatch: final findings may not come until Jun-Dec 2027 (S26), while new JV capacity starts only from FY2028 (S8). A duty imposed first would raise costs before domestic supply is available.
Processors face price volatility. CRGO realisations fell about 18-20% YoY into Q1 FY27 (S13, S25). A duty-led rebound could squeeze processors that cannot pass it through (S12).
Liquidity and concentration: both Vilas and Jay Bee are small caps under Rs 1,000 cr (S18, S19), and Vilas depends on one customer for ~45-55% of sales (S12).
Materiality for JSW Steel: the JV is unlisted, 50%-owned and small relative to group revenue (S7, S21).

method: Weekly refresh of the 2026-W43 edition, researched 30-31 Oct 2026 with web search and direct page fetches. We searched for new DGTR action (none found; DGTR's case page returned 404), Q2/H1 FY27 results for JSW Steel, Vilas, Jay Bee and Mangal (only JSW's were out), Metglas commissioning (not confirmed) and current stock returns. New this week: JSW Steel's Q2 FY27 results (S21) and PL Capital's note (S28); updated stock returns for all three universe names (S18, S19, S20); Mangal's Q1 FY27 CRGO volume and price data (S25); the Rule 17 time limit for DGTR findings (S26); and BIS-licensing context (S27). We dropped the SteelOrbis and Atlanta IPO sources and the Atlanta MVA figure, which are no longer needed. Carried-forward figures (GTRI balance, import mix, JV capex, ICRA, Vilas Q1 and Jay Bee FY26) come from the prior edition's fetched sources; the GTRI, Mondaq, Vilas Q1 and Proterial facts were re-confirmed in this week's searches. The Vilas return page shows inconsistent 6-month and 1-year figures, so both are reported. Source IDs skip S2, S17 and S23. A trade-press snippet says NLMK India, another domestic CRGO producer, was denied domestic-industry standing over links to exporters; we could not open the full text, so it is not used in the body. We found no other listed CRGO steel maker; NLMK India and Shirdi Sai Electricals appear to be unlisted. Voltamp and Shilchar were again left out for lack of a citable CRGO link. Coverage of mid-cap CRGO producers is empty because none exist in the listed universe. Revenue arithmetic is our own and labelled; no ratings or price targets are given.
